modules.module: M1: When the Machine Does Exactly What You Said — and Nothing Like What You Meant

Claude.notes: Opening frame (1880s electrical grid → present-day AI) is one of the strongest analogies in the course. Each of the four lessons opens with a concrete case (CoastRunners, Petrov, Bostrom's paperclip, Anthropic 2022) that cleanly sets up the concept section that follows. Learner is guided to the insight through structured discovery in the labs.
Claude.topIssue: Story-to-concept ratio slightly narrative-heavy for Advanced; lab tutor tends to lead the insight rather than let the learner arrive at it independently.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of Goodhart's Law, reward hacking, instrumental convergence, and specification gaming are technically sound and consistent with the alignment literature (Amodei et al. 2016; Krakovna et al. 2020). RLHF and Constitutional AI descriptions accurate. GPT-4 bar-exam claim (90th percentile) is contested — OpenAI's original figure has been revised downward in follow-up analysis and should be caveated.
Gemini.topIssue: Numerical inconsistency: story text says CoastRunners scored '20% higher than any human player'; quiz feedback for the same case says '28.9% higher'. Only one number can be right.

Perplexity.notes: Real-world cases (CoastRunners, Facebook News Feed, Petrov 1983, Bostrom 2003) remain canonical and continue to be cited in current alignment discourse. Anthropic January 2022 framing still relevant. Lab prompts reference current tools and are executable today.
Perplexity.topIssue: No mention of post-2024 developments — e.g., o1 chain-of-thought reward hacking cases, Anthropic sleeper-agents paper (Hubinger et al. 2024), or the 2025 EU AI Act enforcement phase — that a reader following current AI safety news would expect the intro module to at least gesture at.

modules.module: M2: How AI Systems Develop Unexpected Goals

Claude.notes: The CoastRunners → paperclip → mesa-optimization progression is one of the cleanest narrative arcs in the course: each scene raises a puzzle the next concept section resolves. Actively confronts the misconception that 'AI just does what it's told,' which is the highest-leverage misconception this module could target.
Claude.topIssue: Story labels 'CoastRunners Incident · 1990s Research' — this is a 2016 OpenAI blog post, not 1990s research. The date error weakens the narrative frame even though the case itself is correctly described.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of mesa-optimizer, base optimizer, and deceptive alignment are consistent with Hubinger et al. 2019 'Risks from Learned Optimization.' Instrumental convergence framing aligns with Omohundro 2008 and Bostrom 2014.
Gemini.topIssue: CoastRunners is dated as '1990s Research' — factually wrong (2016). This bleeds into the credibility of every other date in the module and should be corrected before publication.

Perplexity.notes: Mesa-optimization and deceptive alignment are still-live research areas as of late 2025. Bostrom's paperclip thought experiment remains the canonical illustration used by every serious alignment researcher.
Perplexity.topIssue: Anthropic's January 2024 'Sleeper Agents' paper (Hubinger et al.) provides the first empirical demonstration of deceptive alignment behavior in trained models and should be the module's headline current case — its absence is a currency gap.

modules.module: M3: Reward Hacking — When AI Games the Rules

Claude.notes: Atari Tetris and CoastRunners open the module well but the concept section thins out — only 5 key-term definitions, which is lower density than adjacent modules. The 'defenses' lesson could stand more narrative motivation.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative density drops mid-module. Lessons 2 and 3 pivot to expository defense catalogs without the scene-setting cases that made Lesson 1 land.

Gemini.notes: Reward-hacking taxonomy is correct but shallow — only 5 defined key terms, and the distinction between specification gaming, reward tampering, and wireheading is not drawn as cleanly as the literature does (Krakovna et al. 2020; Everitt et al. 2021). Atari Tetris date '1999' is defensible but the more commonly cited Tetris pause-and-hold exploit was formalized later (Lehman et al. 2019, 'The Surprising Creativity of Digital Evolution').
Gemini.topIssue: The 'Defenses Against Reward Hacking' lesson lists techniques (impact regularization, quantilization, adversarial training) without indicating which are theoretical vs. empirically demonstrated to work at scale.

Perplexity.notes: Classic cases are still valid touchstones. Deployed-system framing lets the reader connect toy examples to production systems they interact with daily.
Perplexity.topIssue: Recent reward-hacking incidents — o1's chain-of-thought exploits (OpenAI 2024), Claude's opus-3 evaluation gaming behaviors, and DeepSeek-R1 reward hacking observations — are the current evidence base and are entirely missing.

modules.module: M4: Human Feedback and Its Limitations

Claude.notes: The 2022 turning point → 2023 sycophancy findings arc gives RLHF a genuine story, not a procedure diagram. Sycophancy lesson lets the learner discover the failure mode rather than being told 'RLHF has this bug.'
Claude.topIssue: Lesson 3 'Scaling Failures' resolves too quickly — the story sets up a big open question and the concept section wraps it with three bullet points.

Gemini.notes: RLHF pipeline described consistent with Christiano et al. 2017 and Ouyang et al. 2022 (InstructGPT). Sycophancy framing aligns with Sharma et al. 2023 (Anthropic) 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models.' Rater-inconsistency numbers are within published ranges.
Gemini.topIssue: The claim that 'inter-rater agreement runs 60-70%' is a common cited figure but Anthropic's own Constitutional AI paper reports higher agreement in well-calibrated pools — the range as stated is technically defensible but reads as universal when it isn't.

Perplexity.notes: Sycophancy research through 2024 is well represented. RLHF-to-DPO transition mentioned. Content holds up against 2025 developments.
Perplexity.topIssue: RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) and Constitutional AI 2.0 are current alternatives to RLHF that would give the 'future of feedback' lesson a real answer rather than an open question.

modules.module: M5: Interpretability — Looking Inside the Machine

Claude.notes: Induction-heads discovery is the perfect opening scene for interpretability — a real result that made the field suddenly feel tractable. 16 defined key terms is the highest density in the course, appropriate for the topic.
Claude.topIssue: Lab executability is the module's weak point — 'work with the tutor to reason about circuits' cannot replicate the actual experience of using an SAE dashboard or a neuron-visualization tool.

Gemini.notes: Circuits and features terminology accurate per Elhage et al. 2021 'A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits' and Olsson et al. 2022 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads.' Sycophancy-in-hidden-representations link is a fair characterization of Sharma et al. 2023.
Gemini.topIssue: Descriptions of 'features' and 'monosemanticity' predate Anthropic's May 2024 Scaling Monosemanticity paper, which meaningfully changed what interpretability researchers claim is possible. The framing feels 2023-vintage.

Perplexity.notes: Induction heads is still cited as the foundational interpretability result. The 'limits and challenges' lesson honestly notes the field's open state.
Perplexity.topIssue: SAE / dictionary-learning breakthroughs (Cunningham et al. 2023, Anthropic's Scaling Monosemanticity 2024, Golden Gate Claude 2024) are the current headline results — a module on interpretability written for an Advanced audience in 2025-2026 that omits them reads dated.

modules.module: M6: Governance and Global Safety Efforts

Claude.notes: Bletchley Park opening (Turing's Enigma site now hosting AI safety diplomacy) is the module's best narrative move. The four historical anchor scenes (EU AI Act, Bletchley, White House commitments, FLI open letter) each set up a lesson cleanly.
Claude.topIssue: Delivery architecture is muddled — 11 h1 headings across 'lessons,' 'checks,' and 'workshops' break the story→concept→quiz→lab rhythm that the rest of the course uses. Learner orientation suffers.

Gemini.notes: EU AI Act classifications (real-time biometric surveillance as prohibited under Article 5) accurate. Executive Order 14110 requirements — accurate. Bletchley Declaration participant list and content accurate. Seoul Summit May 2024 commitments correctly cited.
Gemini.topIssue: The distinction between 'binding' and 'voluntary' international commitments could be sharpened — the module treats the Bletchley Declaration as more consequential than it legally is.

Perplexity.notes: This is the freshest module in the course — content spans through the 2024 Seoul summit. EU AI Act enforcement timeline, US EO 14110 (and its later rescission and replacement under the 2025 administration) is close to current.
Perplexity.topIssue: Executive Order 14110 was rescinded in January 2025 by EO 14179; the module still presents 14110 as active US policy, which is now factually stale.

Claude.notes: Power-seeking and deceptive-alignment framing is coherent, but Lesson 2 covers ground already established in M2, and the reader notices. The narrative doesn't quite justify why catastrophic risk needs its own module vs. an extension of M2.
Claude.topIssue: 'Documented Case — 2016' as a scene label is vague; a specific incident name would make the scene land harder.

Gemini.notes: Power-seeking argument aligns with Turner et al. 2021 'Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power.' Deceptive alignment definitions consistent with earlier modules and with Hubinger et al. 2019. Risk-scenario framing draws from Bostrom, Yudkowsky, Christiano.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'large-scale risk scenarios' lesson mixes empirical alignment failures with speculative existential-risk arguments without flagging which is which — an Advanced learner needs that epistemic separation to reason about the claims.

Perplexity.notes: Framing is broadly current but the empirical evidence base has moved on. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and the AI 2027 report are the current touchstones for how the field talks about catastrophic risk in 2025-2026.
Perplexity.topIssue: The module presents catastrophic risk as an inference from theory (Bostrom, Omohundro) when the empirical case now rests on 2024-2025 evaluations of capability elicitation (biosecurity uplift, autonomous replication, deceptive behavior) — none of which are cited.

modules.module: M8: What Individuals Can Do About AI Safety

Claude.notes: Strongest applied module in the course. The story creates the problem (individual action feels futile in the face of trillion-dollar labs) and each lesson gives the reader a concrete, doable action. Capability delta is unambiguous.
Claude.topIssue: The 'historical context' scene is thinner than other module openings — one more concrete anchor (e.g., a specific red-team finding or civic AI campaign win) would strengthen it.

Gemini.notes: GPT-4 red-teaming description consistent with OpenAI's GPT-4 System Card and the ARC Evals write-up. Reporting mechanisms (Anthropic responsible disclosure, OpenAI bug bounty) are correctly described.
Gemini.topIssue: 'Building a personal AI safety practice' lesson is prescriptive without citing the evidence base for any of the recommended practices — it reads more advocacy than analysis.

Perplexity.notes: Civic-engagement pathways (UK AI Safety Institute, US AISI, state-level legislation like California SB 1047) are actively evolving; module tone is current. Red-teaming programs at Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind are correctly framed as ongoing.
Perplexity.topIssue: California SB 1047 was vetoed in September 2024 and the current legislative landscape (Colorado AI Act, Texas TRAIGA, EU AI Act enforcement) is not reflected — the civic-engagement lesson is where currency matters most and it needs a refresh.
